The Majority Standard Bible — translated from this same Greek text — renders it “found fault” in 1 of those places (33%), e.g. Mark 7:2. This is observed translation data, not an editorial opinion.
The Berean Standard Bible, an independent translation, agrees with that rendering in 0% of the same verses.

prose.def: To blame or find fault with someone, used of both ordinary human criticism and God's judgment against people or a covenant.
senseLabels: to find fault with someone (accusative object)
prose.article: μέμφομαι means to blame, criticize, or find fault, and all three of its New Testament uses point to that single core idea even though the translations are worded differently ("found fault," "God find fault," "fault"). It's a common everyday word in the papyri: one letter complains "I blame you greatly for the loss of two pigs," and another says "I blame the person who told you," showing how ordinary the term was. In the Septuagint it appears only a handful of times (Sirach 11:7, 41:7, and 2 Maccabees 2:7).
prose.caution: This word is rare, appearing only 3 times in the Byzantine New Testament (2 in the critical text), so its measured range rests on thin evidence.

issues: Sense labels 1 and 3 are identical ('to find fault') despite mapping to different verses (MAR 7:2 and HEB 8:8), obscuring that HEB 8:8 uses the word with an accusative object (God finding fault with the people/covenant) while MAR 7:2 is an absolute or different construction

Syntactic roles show 'vocative (2×)' which is unexpected for a verb — this likely reflects a parsing anomaly but the definition does not acknowledge any morphological or constructional variation (absolute use vs. accusative object)

The definition's phrasing 'someone or something' is adequate but the article claims all three uses point to a 'single core idea' without noting that ROM 9:19 frames the subject as God objecting to humans, a theologically distinct coloring worth flagging
BSB independently agrees 0% for senses 1 and 3, signaling translation divergence the definition should at least gesture toward

receipts.how: Paul uses μέμφομαι absolutely ('God find fault') to raise a rhetorical objection about divine judgment, showing the word can express a theological challenge to God's right to blame, directly fitting the core definition.

The author uses μέμφομαι with an accusative object (αὐτούς) meaning God finds fault with the covenant people, demonstrating the accusative construction the Abbott-Smith note flags and which the current definition does not distinguish from the absolute use.

Mark uses μέμφομαι in the sense of finding fault with the disciples for eating with unwashed hands, the most everyday, non-theological use, confirming the definition's core gloss but also showing BSB rendered it differently (0% independent agreement).

audit.author_note: Paul (ROM 9:19) deploys μέμφομαι in an abstract theological argument about divine justice, while Hebrews (HEB 8:8) uses it with a specific accusative object in a cultic-covenantal context, and Mark (MAR 7:2) uses it in a straightforward social criticism scene — readers of each author will encounter a subtly different register.

prose.def: A person who complains about their fate or lot in life; a grumbler or malcontent (used as a plural noun at Jude 1:16).
prose.article: This adjective describes someone who finds fault with their fate or lot, the grumbler who is never satisfied. It appears just once in the New Testament, in Jude 1:16, where the Majority Standard Bible and BSB both render the surrounding phrase the same way. The word is built from μέμφομαι (to blame) plus μοῖρα (fate, lot), and Moulton-Milligan notes a related form ἀμεμψιμοίρητος ('blameless') in a papyrus from 164 B.C.; the term also turns up meaning 'censorious' in the astrologer Vettius Valens.
prose.caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its precise range rests on slim evidence supplemented by a few outside attestations.

classical.lsj: μεμψῐ́-μοιρος , ον , faultfinding, criticizing, querulous , Isoc. 12.8 , Thphr. Char. 17.2 , Phld. Lib. p.42 O., Ep.Jud. 16 , Luc. Tim. 13 , etc.; τὸ μ. Plu. 2.50b : Comp. , γυνὴ ἀνδρὸς -ότερον Arist. HA 608b10 .

issues: The sense label '1. own' is a data artifact and does not describe the actual meaning; it should be labeled something like 'grumbler / fault-finder with one's fate'
The definition calls the word an adjective in the article, but it functions as a noun (plural substantive μεμψίμοιροι) in JUD 1:16, meaning 'complainers' as persons, not a descriptive modifier
The definition phrase 'habitually' is not supported by the single NT occurrence or the classical lexicons, which give no iterative force beyond the word's inherent character
The existing caution is appropriate but the article slightly overstates the MSB/BSB rendering agreement as independently meaningful given there is only one occurrence

receipts.how: The sole NT occurrence uses μεμψίμοιροι as a substantive plural noun meaning 'complainers' (people who blame their fate), confirming the core meaning but demonstrating the word acts as a noun, not an adjective modifier.

Classical lexicons (Abbott-Smith, Dodson, Strong's) all gloss this verse as 'complaining of one's fate / querulous / discontented,' supporting the definition's core sense of fault-finding with one's lot.

Moulton-Milligan connects μεμψίμοιροι here to the querulosi of the Assumption of Moses, showing the word denotes a recognized character type of grumbler, not merely situational complaint, which slightly qualifies the word 'habitually' in the current definition as unsupported by NT evidence alone.
